profile.campus: Palo Alto, California (Equinix SV8 / Palo Alto Internet Exchange)
profile.reading:
This is Equinix's SV8 facility at 529 Bryant Street in Palo Alto, California, also known by the OSM alt-name Palo Alto Internet Exchange, reflecting its role as an early peering point in Silicon Valley's internet infrastructure. Equinix's own published specifications describe SV8 as a three-story, reinforced-concrete building of 26,296 square feet, with N+1 power and cooling redundancy, a minimum cabinet density of 2kVA, 120v/208v power distribution, a 99.9999%-plus global guaranteed uptime commitment, and certifications including ISO 27001, HIPAA, and PCI DSS. Equinix markets SV8 as serving what it calls the largest concentration of high-tech companies and peering hubs in the world, with access to important financial and enterprise ecosystems. Equinix, founded in Silicon Valley in 1998 by former Digital Equipment Corporation facilities managers Al Avery and Jay Adelson on the premise of providing a neutral place for competing networks to interconnect, remains headquartered nearby in Redwood City; the Palo Alto location's downtown setting, distinct from the larger Great Oaks and Corvin Drive campuses in San Jose and Santa Clara, reflects its historical role as an internet exchange point rather than a large-scale colocation campus. Equinix converted to a real estate investment trust in January 2015 and trades on Nasdaq as EQIX. Equinix's SV8 page did not disclose a specific founding or opening date for the Palo Alto facility in the material fetched this session.

Palo Alto's own municipal electric utility, one of the few Bay Area cities with a city-owned power system, has periodically weighed in on the demands large downtown facilities like SV8 place on its distribution grid, a different regulatory relationship than the investor-owned PG&E service most other Silicon Valley Equinix buildings rely on.

reading.body:
Equinix SV8 in Palo Alto is a 26,296 square foot colocation facility with N+1 redundancy across power, cooling, and generators, but its actual power capacity in megawatts remains unpublished.

The lack of published MW figures for individual facilities obscures how much compute capacity Equinix can actually serve in Silicon Valley. SV8 is one of twelve facilities in the region that collectively claim to serve over 10,500 customers, yet the power envelope for each building is invisible to outside analysis. This matters because AI workloads are power-constrained, and colocation pricing and availability depend on whether a facility has spare power to allocate. Without capacity figures, one cannot assess whether Silicon Valley's largest retail colocation footprint has headroom for additional AI compute or is already power-limited.

N+1 redundancy means the facility can tolerate one simultaneous failure in any of three critical systems without service loss. This is standard practice for enterprise colocation but does not indicate whether the facility is designed for the continuous, intensive power draw of modern AI training or inference clusters. The redundancy tier and square footage tell you the facility exists and meets baseline availability requirements. They do not tell you its thermal design, power density per rack, or whether its cooling systems can handle the heat signatures of GPUs and custom accelerators that now dominate customer demand.
